Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush signed an executive order Friday expanding U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe, the White House said. About 200 victims of election violence seek safety outside the U.S. Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, this month. "The new executive order significantly enhances our ability to designate individuals in and entities connected to the Mugabe regime," Bush said in a written statement that calls the Zimbabwean government under president Robert Mugabe "illegitimate." Just after the announcement, the Treasury Department said it has designated for sanctions 17 entities, including three government-owned or controlled companies used by Mugabe and his government "to illegally siphon revenue and foreign exchange from the Zimbabwean people," as well as one individual. "This action is a direct result of the Mugabe regime's continued politically motivated violence, disregarding calls from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the United Nations to halt the attacks," the White House said. "The regime has also continued its ban against NGO activities that would provide assistance to the suffering and vulnerable people of Zimbabwe. No regime should ignore the will of its own people and calls from the international community without consequences." The U.S. has been pushing for sanctions against Zimbabwe since Mugabe ignored a U.N. Security Council appeal to postpone a presidential runoff election June 27. The vote initially was intended to be a runoff between Mugabe and opposition candidate Morgan Tsvangirai, who did not win the presidency outright in the general election, according to government tallies. But Tsvangirai, of the Movement for Democratic Change, withdrew just before the vote, saying Mugabe's supporters had orchestrated a campaign of beatings, intimidation and murders against Tsvangirai supporters. Earlier this month, Russia and China vetoed a Security Council resolution pushed by the United States, Britain and France that would have imposed international sanctions on Mugabe and senior members of his government. Bush said last week he was "displeased" at the vetoes, but the Treasury and State Departments were working on potential U.S. action. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Jendayi Frazer told members of Congress last week that more than 100 people have been murdered, more than 3,000 have been injured by beatings or torture and more than 30,000 have been driven from their homes because of violence that broke out after the general election. Entities designated by the Treasury Department include Minerals Marketing Corp. of Zimbabwe, the company that serves as the sole marketing and export agent for all minerals mined in Zimbabwe except gold and silver; Zimbabwe Mining Development Corp.; and Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Co., among others. The individual named is Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari. The Treasury Department said he is an Omani national who has close ties to Mugabe and his top officials and uses his company, Oryx Natural Resources, to "enable Mugabe ... to maintain access to, and derive personal benefit from, various mining ventures in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Under the sanctions, any assets tied to al-Shanfari or to the designated companies that are within U.S. jurisdictions must be frozen, and people living in the United States are prohibited from doing business with them. On Monday, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an agreement that paves the way for power-sharing talks to take place in the next few weeks. They will be mediated by South African President Thabo Mbeki, as a representative of the Southern African Development Community, and Jean Ping, chairman of the African Union Commission. Bush said Friday the United States is ready to provide a "substantial assistance package, development aid and normalization with international financial institutions" should those talks result in a new government "that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people." In the meantime, the president said he is authorizing the use of up to $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to assist Zimbabwean refugees and those displaced by the violence. In addition, he said the United States will continue efforts to provide food and medical care to Zimbabweans.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Bush signed an executive order Friday expanding U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe, the White House said.

About 200 victims of election-related violence sought safety outside the U.S. Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, this month.

“The new executive order significantly enhances our ability to designate individuals and entities connected to the Mugabe regime,” Bush said in a written statement, which described the Zimbabwean government under President Robert Mugabe as “illegitimate.”

Shortly after the announcement, the Treasury Department said it had designated 17 entities and one individual for sanctions. The entities include three government-owned or government-controlled companies used by Mugabe and his government “to illegally siphon revenue and foreign exchange from the Zimbabwean people.”

“This action is a direct result of the Mugabe regime’s continued politically motivated violence, disregarding calls from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the United Nations to halt the attacks,” the White House said.

“The regime has also continued its ban against NGO activities that would provide assistance to the suffering and vulnerable people of Zimbabwe. No regime should ignore the will of its own people and calls from the international community without consequences.”

The United States has been pressing for sanctions against Zimbabwe since Mugabe ignored a U.N. Security Council appeal to postpone the June 27 presidential runoff election.

The vote was initially intended to be a runoff between Mugabe and opposition candidate Morgan Tsvangirai, who, according to government tallies, did not win the presidency outright in the general election. But Tsvangirai, leader of the Movement for Democratic Change, withdrew shortly before the vote, saying Mugabe’s supporters had orchestrated a campaign of beatings, intimidation and murder against his supporters.

Earlier this month, Russia and China vetoed a Security Council resolution advanced by the United States, Britain and France that would have imposed international sanctions on Mugabe and senior members of his government.

Bush said last week that he was “displeased” by the vetoes, but that the Treasury and State departments were considering potential U.S. action.

Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Jendayi Frazer told members of Congress last week that more than 100 people had been murdered, more than 3,000 had been injured through beatings or torture, and more than 30,000 had been driven from their homes because of violence that erupted after the general election.

The entities designated by the Treasury Department include Minerals Marketing Corp. of Zimbabwe, which serves as the sole marketing and export agent for all minerals mined in Zimbabwe except gold and silver; Zimbabwe Mining Development Corp.; and Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Co., among others.

The individual designated is Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari. The Treasury Department said he is an Omani national with close ties to Mugabe and his top officials who uses his company, Oryx Natural Resources, to “enable Mugabe ... to maintain access to, and derive personal benefit from, various mining ventures in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.”

Under the sanctions, any assets tied to al-Shanfari or the designated companies that fall within U.S. jurisdiction must be frozen, and people living in the United States are prohibited from doing business with them.

On Monday, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an agreement paving the way for power-sharing talks to take place within the next few weeks. The talks will be mediated by South African President Thabo Mbeki, representing the Southern African Development Community, and Jean Ping, chairman of the African Union Commission.

Bush said Friday that the United States is prepared to provide a “substantial assistance package, development aid and normalization with international financial institutions” if the talks result in a new government “that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people.”

In the meantime, Bush said he is authorizing the use of up to $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to assist Zimbabwean refugees and people displaced by the violence.

He added that the United States would continue its efforts to provide food and medical care to Zimbabweans.
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — The White House announced that President Bush signed an executive order Friday broadening U.S. sanctions on Zimbabwe.

Earlier this month, roughly 200 people fleeing election-related violence sought protection outside the U.S. Embassy in Harare.

In a written statement, Bush described President Robert Mugabe’s government as illegitimate and said the order would greatly increase Washington’s ability to target people and organizations associated with Mugabe’s administration.

Soon after the announcement, the Treasury Department imposed sanctions on 17 organizations and one person. The listed entities include three state-owned or state-controlled companies that, according to U.S. officials, were used by Mugabe and his government to unlawfully divert revenue and foreign currency from Zimbabwe’s population.

The White House said the measures were prompted by the Mugabe government’s ongoing politically driven violence and its refusal to heed demands from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the United Nations to stop the attacks. It also criticized the continuing prohibition on nongovernmental organizations carrying out work intended to help Zimbabwe’s vulnerable and suffering citizens. The administration said governments should face consequences when they disregard both their own people’s wishes and appeals from the international community.

The United States had sought sanctions against Zimbabwe after Mugabe rejected a U.N. Security Council request to delay the June 27 presidential runoff.

The election was originally supposed to pit Mugabe against opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai. Official results from the general election showed that Tsvangirai had failed to secure the presidency outright. However, the Movement for Democratic Change leader withdrew shortly before the runoff, alleging that Mugabe supporters had organized killings, beatings and intimidation targeting his followers.

Earlier in the month, Russia and China blocked a Security Council resolution backed by the United States, Britain and France that would have established international sanctions against Mugabe and high-ranking officials in his government.

Bush said the previous week that he was unhappy with those vetoes, while noting that the State and Treasury departments were considering possible unilateral U.S. measures.

Jendayi Frazer, the assistant secretary of state for African affairs, told Congress the previous week that violence following the general election had killed more than 100 people, left over 3,000 injured through torture or beatings and forced more than 30,000 from their homes.

Among the organizations sanctioned by the Treasury Department were the Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe, which is the exclusive marketing and export agency for every mineral mined in the country apart from gold and silver; the Zimbabwe Mining Development Corporation; and the Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Company.

The sole individual named was Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari. Treasury officials identified him as an Omani citizen with close connections to Mugabe and senior members of his administration. They said al-Shanfari used his business, Oryx Natural Resources, to help Mugabe retain access to mining projects in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and personally profit from them.

The sanctions require that assets belonging to al-Shanfari or the named companies be frozen if they fall under U.S. jurisdiction. People residing in the United States are also barred from conducting business with them.

On Monday, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an accord establishing a path toward power-sharing negotiations expected to occur within the following several weeks. The discussions were to be mediated by South African President Thabo Mbeki on behalf of the Southern African Development Community, together with African Union Commission Chairman Jean Ping.

Bush said Friday that if the negotiations produced a government representing the wishes of Zimbabwe’s population, the United States would be prepared to offer significant assistance, including development support and normalized relations with international financial institutions.

Until then, Bush authorized as much as $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to help Zimbabwean refugees and people uprooted by the violence. He added that Washington would continue working to supply Zimbabweans with food and medical assistance.

President George W. Bush expanded U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe, signing an executive order aimed at individuals and organizations associated with President Robert Mugabe’s government. The measure broadened Washington’s authority to freeze assets under U.S. jurisdiction and prohibit Americans from conducting business with those accused of undermining democratic institutions, participating in political violence or supporting the Mugabe administration.

The action followed Zimbabwe’s disputed 2008 presidential election. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai won more votes than Mugabe in the first round but officially fell short of the majority required to avoid a runoff. Tsvangirai later withdrew from the second round, citing widespread attacks, intimidation and killings directed at opposition supporters. Mugabe proceeded with the vote and was declared the winner, although the election was widely condemned as neither free nor fair.

The Bush administration also criticized Zimbabwean authorities for repressing political opponents and imposing restrictions on humanitarian organizations. Those restrictions disrupted aid efforts at a time when the country was facing severe food shortages, economic collapse and soaring inflation.

Alongside the executive order, the Treasury Department designated 17 entities and one individual for sanctions, identifying them as connected to or controlled by the Zimbabwean government. Any assets held by those targets within U.S. jurisdiction were frozen, and U.S. citizens and companies were generally barred from engaging in transactions with them.

Bush said the United States would continue to pressure Mugabe’s government and support Zimbabweans seeking democratic change. The expanded sanctions were designed to focus on government leaders and their financial networks rather than the broader population, which was already suffering from the country’s political and economic crisis.

The move also reflected frustration over the failure of the United Nations Security Council to impose wider international penalties. Russia and China had vetoed a proposed resolution that would have placed sanctions on Mugabe and other senior officials. With broader U.N. action blocked, the United States chose to strengthen its own measures against the regime and encouraged other governments to take similar steps.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about President George W. Bush expanding U.S. sanctions against Robert Mugabe’s government in Zimbabwe following election violence.
counterfactuals.output:
**Bush expands U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe after election violence**

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style report)** — President George W. Bush has expanded U.S. sanctions against the government of Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, citing political violence and intimidation surrounding the country’s disputed presidential election.

The measures broaden Washington’s authority to freeze the U.S.-based assets of Zimbabwean officials, government-controlled businesses and others accused of undermining democratic institutions or supporting repression.

“This action is a direct response to the Mugabe regime’s continued assault on its own people and institutions,” the White House said.

Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai withdrew from the June 2008 presidential runoff, saying attacks against his supporters made a free and fair vote impossible. Mugabe proceeded as the only candidate and was declared the winner, but the election was widely condemned by Western governments and international observers.

Zimbabwean authorities have blamed the opposition for unrest and rejected foreign criticism as interference in the country’s internal affairs.

The United States had already imposed travel restrictions and targeted financial sanctions on Mugabe and senior members of his government. The expanded order allows the Treasury Department to target a wider network of individuals and companies linked to the leadership.

Bush also called for stronger international pressure on Harare. Efforts to impose United Nations sanctions, however, faced resistance from Russia and China, which argued that the crisis did not constitute a threat to international peace and security.

The political turmoil comes as Zimbabwe struggles with hyperinflation, food shortages and widespread unemployment. Regional leaders have continued to press Mugabe’s ruling party and Tsvangirai’s opposition movement to negotiate a power-sharing agreement.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the United States’ decision to impose additional sanctions on Zimbabwe, including the targeted entities, the political context, and planned humanitarian assistance.
counterfactuals.output:
The United States replaced its broad Zimbabwe-specific sanctions program with narrower Global Magnitsky sanctions aimed at people and businesses accused of corruption or serious human-rights abuses.

The measures targeted 11 individuals, including President Emmerson Mnangagwa, first lady Auxillia Mnangagwa, Vice President Constantino Chiwenga, senior security and government officials, and businessman Kudakwashe Tagwirei and members of his network. Three Tagwirei-linked companies—Sakunda Holdings, Fossil Agro and Fossil Contracting—were also targeted.

Washington tied the action to entrenched corruption, repression of political opponents and civil society, and abuses surrounding Zimbabwe’s disputed August 2023 election, which returned Mnangagwa to office but was criticized by domestic and international observers as failing democratic standards. U.S. officials stressed that the sanctions were directed at specific actors, not Zimbabwe’s population.

Separately, the United States said it planned more than $20 million in additional humanitarian food assistance to help Zimbabweans facing severe hunger worsened by drought and the El Niño weather pattern.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article on Bush’s executive order strengthening sanctions against Zimbabwe after Russia and China vetoed a related U.N. Security Council resolution.
counterfactuals.output:
**Bush strengthens Zimbabwe sanctions after Russia and China block U.N. action**

**WASHINGTON, July 25, 2008** — President George W. Bush ordered an expansion of U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe on Friday, two weeks after Russia and China vetoed a proposed United Nations Security Council resolution that would have imposed international penalties on President Robert Mugabe and members of his government.

The executive order broadens Washington’s authority to freeze assets held under U.S. jurisdiction by Zimbabwean officials, government-controlled businesses and other people or organizations accused of supporting political repression, corruption or attacks on democratic institutions. It also bars Americans from conducting transactions involving property blocked under the order.

Bush said the measure was a response to violence and intimidation surrounding Zimbabwe’s disputed presidential election.

“This action is a direct result of the Mugabe regime’s continued politically motivated violence,” the president said in announcing the order. He said the United States would act against government-linked individuals and entities involved in undermining democracy in Zimbabwe.

The order expands sanctions first imposed by Bush in 2003 and widened in 2005. Those earlier measures targeted Mugabe and senior members of his administration. The latest directive gives the Treasury Department broader authority to designate additional officials, companies and financial networks linked to the government.

Among those potentially subject to sanctions are senior Zimbabwean officials; people responsible for human-rights abuses connected to political repression; officials involved in public corruption; and individuals or companies that provide financial, technological or other support to sanctioned figures. Businesses owned or controlled by designated people can also be targeted.

The action does not amount to a general trade embargo against Zimbabwe. Instead, it is intended to isolate Mugabe’s leadership and its financial supporters while limiting the effect on ordinary Zimbabweans, who are already struggling with economic collapse, severe food shortages and extraordinarily high inflation.

### Action follows Security Council veto

The U.S. move followed the July 11 defeat of a Security Council resolution sponsored by the United States and Britain. The proposal would have imposed an arms embargo on Zimbabwe and travel bans and asset freezes on Mugabe and 13 other senior officials.

Nine of the council’s 15 members voted for the resolution, enough to meet the numerical requirement for passage. But Russia and China, both permanent members with veto power, voted against it, preventing its adoption. Libya, South Africa and Vietnam also opposed the measure, while Indonesia abstained.

Supporters of the resolution argued that the Zimbabwean government’s campaign of violence after the first round of presidential voting had become a threat to regional stability and required an international response.

Russia and China contended that Zimbabwe’s turmoil was an internal political matter and did not constitute a threat to international peace and security—the standard basis for mandatory Security Council sanctions. South Africa, which was leading regional mediation, argued that punitive action could undermine negotiations between Mugabe’s ZANU-PF party and the opposition Movement for Democratic Change.

The veto frustrated the Bush administration, which had pushed for multilateral sanctions after Mugabe proceeded with a June 27 presidential runoff from which opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai had withdrawn.

### Disputed election and violence

Zimbabwe’s crisis intensified after elections on March 29. Official results showed Tsvangirai finishing ahead of Mugabe in the presidential contest but short of the majority required to avoid a runoff. The results were not released for more than a month, fueling opposition allegations that the government was manipulating the count.

In the weeks before the runoff, opposition supporters faced widespread assaults, arrests, displacement and intimidation. Tsvangirai withdrew several days before the vote, saying the level of violence made a free election impossible and that participating would endanger his supporters.

Mugabe remained the only active candidate and was declared the winner. He was sworn in for another term shortly afterward. Western governments and many election observers rejected the runoff as illegitimate.

Human-rights groups and the opposition blamed state security forces, ruling-party activists and pro-government militias for much of the violence. Mugabe’s government accused the opposition of provoking unrest and acting on behalf of Britain, the former colonial power, and other Western governments.

Mugabe, who has led Zimbabwe since independence in 1980, has repeatedly described U.S. and European sanctions as an attempt to overthrow his government. His administration has also blamed the penalties for the country’s economic decline. Washington maintains that the measures are aimed at political leaders and their associates, not Zimbabwe’s population, and says economic mismanagement and government policies are primarily responsible for the crisis.

### Pressure alongside negotiations

Bush’s order came as ZANU-PF and the opposition began talks aimed at negotiating a political settlement. Earlier in the week, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an agreement establishing a framework for negotiations under the mediation of South African President Thabo Mbeki.

The talks were expected to address the possibility of a power-sharing arrangement, constitutional changes and measures to end political violence. Major differences remained over who would exercise executive authority and whether Mugabe’s disputed reelection would be recognized.

The United States said it supported a negotiated settlement but insisted that any agreement must reflect the March election results and the will of Zimbabwean voters. By strengthening unilateral sanctions, the Bush administration signaled that it would continue applying financial pressure even without Security Council authorization.

Under the executive order, the Treasury Department can add names and entities to its sanctions list without seeking further legislation. Any assets they hold in the United States—or that pass through U.S. financial institutions—can be frozen, and American banks and companies generally must refuse transactions involving them.

The practical effect depends in part on whether targeted officials and businesses use dollars, maintain overseas accounts or conduct business through institutions exposed to the U.S. financial system. Even when sanctioned parties hold few assets in the United States, designation can make international banks and companies reluctant to deal with them.

The order therefore represents both a direct financial penalty and an effort to increase Mugabe’s diplomatic and commercial isolation following the failure to secure binding action at the United Nations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the U.S. response to Zimbabwe’s disputed 2008 presidential runoff, covering violence against Morgan Tsvangirai’s supporters, Treasury sanctions, and proposed power-sharing talks.
counterfactuals.output:
The United States treated Zimbabwe’s June 27, 2008 presidential runoff as illegitimate. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai had won more votes than President Robert Mugabe in the March election but, according to official results, not enough to avoid a runoff. Before the second round, security forces and ZANU-PF militias conducted a campaign of beatings, killings, arrests, intimidation, and displacement aimed largely at Tsvangirai’s Movement for Democratic Change supporters. Tsvangirai withdrew, saying participation would expose voters to further violence, and briefly took refuge in the Dutch embassy. Washington described the resulting one-candidate vote and Mugabe’s inauguration as a “sham” that did not express the Zimbabwean people’s will.

The U.S. response included:

- **Diplomatic pressure:** The Bush administration refused to regard the runoff as conferring legitimate authority on Mugabe. It pushed for international condemnation, supported African Union and regional mediation, and backed a U.N. Security Council sanctions resolution, although Russia and China vetoed it in July 2008.
- **Treasury sanctions:** Using an expanded executive order, the Treasury Department tightened targeted financial sanctions against people and entities supporting Mugabe’s government or undermining democratic institutions. It froze U.S.-linked assets and prohibited transactions with designated state-controlled businesses, including mining, financial, and development enterprises. Washington emphasized that these were targeted measures against the ruling network, not a general embargo on Zimbabweans.
- **Conditional support for power sharing:** The United States was open to talks between ZANU-PF and the MDC, led regionally by South African President Thabo Mbeki, but argued that negotiations had to reflect the March election results and could not simply legitimize Mugabe’s violent runoff. U.S. officials called for an end to political violence, release of detainees, restoration of humanitarian access, and a transitional or power-sharing arrangement in which Tsvangirai and the MDC exercised genuine governing authority.

Those negotiations ultimately produced the September 2008 Global Political Agreement, under which Mugabe remained president and Tsvangirai later became prime minister. The United States remained skeptical and kept sanctions in place, judging implementation by whether real power was shared and repression ended.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a wire-service report describing new American sanctions on Mugabe-linked companies and individuals, why they were imposed, how they work, and what support Washington offered Zimbabweans.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON, [date] (Reuters)** — The United States imposed new sanctions on companies and individuals linked to Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, accusing them of helping his government undermine democracy, commit political violence and plunder state resources.

The Treasury Department said the measures target senior officials, government-controlled businesses and commercial networks that provide financial or material support to Mugabe and his allies. Washington has blamed the government for repression surrounding disputed elections, attacks on opposition supporters and policies that contributed to Zimbabwe’s economic collapse.

The sanctions freeze any assets the designated people or companies hold under U.S. jurisdiction and generally bar Americans and U.S. businesses from dealing with them. Financial institutions also risk penalties if they process prohibited transactions involving those named.

U.S. officials described the restrictions as targeted measures rather than a broad trade embargo, saying they were intended to pressure the ruling elite without punishing ordinary Zimbabweans.

Washington said it would continue humanitarian assistance, including food and health aid, while supporting civil society, independent media and democratic institutions. It also offered to help Zimbabwe rebuild its economy and public services if its leaders restored political freedoms, respected human rights and moved toward credible democratic government.
